# Using the GDB Debugger {#appendix-f-using-the-gdb-debugger}

By the time you read this appendix, you will likely have written at
least one program with an error in it. In assembly language, even minor
errors usually have results such as the whole program crashing with a
segmentation fault error. In most programming languages, you can simply
print out the values in your variables as you go along, and use that
output to find out where you went wrong. In assembly language, calling
output functions is not so easy. Therefore, to aid in determining the
source of errors, you must use a *source debugger*.

A debugger is a program that helps you find bugs by stepping through the
program one step at a time, letting you examine memory and register
contents along the way. A *source debugger* is a debugger that allows
you to tie the debugging operation directly to the source code of a
program. This means that the debugger allows you to look at the source
code as you typed it in - complete with symbols, labels, and comments.

The debugger we will be looking at is GDB - the GNU Debugger. This
application is present on almost all GNU/Linux distributions. It can
debug programs in multiple programming languages, including assembly
language.

An Example Debugging Session {#an-example-debugging-session}
----------------------------

The best way to explain how a debugger works is by using it. The program
we will be using the debugger on is the `003-02-maximum` program used in
[Chapter 3. Your First Programs](03-your-first-programs.qmd#chapter-3-your-first-programs).
Let\'s say that you entered the program perfectly, except that you left
out the line:

```{.gnuassembler}
incq %rcx               # Increment %rcx by 1.
```

When you run the program, it just goes in an infinite loop - it never
exits. To determine the cause, you need to run the program under GDB.
However, to do this, you need to have the assembler include debugging
information in the executable. All you need to do to enable this is to
add the `-g` option to the `as` command, as we have done in every
program of this book. So, you would assemble it like this:

```{.bash}
as --64 -g -o 003-02-maximum.o 003-02-maximum.s
ld -o 003-02-maximum 003-02-maximum.o
```

Linking would be the same as normal. The debugging information (in the
DWARF format, which gdb reads) tells the debugger which line of the
source file each instruction comes from. Now, to run the program under
the debugger, you would type in `gdb ./003-02-maximum`. Be sure that the
source files are in the current directory. GDB prints its version and a
few lines about its license and its help, and then:

    Reading symbols from ./003-02-maximum...
    (gdb)

The sessions in this appendix were made with GDB 15.1 on Ubuntu 24.04.
Depending on which version of GDB you are running, the output may vary
slightly. At this point, the program is loaded, but is not running yet.
The debugger is waiting your command. To run your program, just type in
`run`. This will not return, because the program is running in an
infinite loop. To stop the program, hit `control-c`. The screen will
then say this:

    Program received signal SIGINT, Interrupt.
    _start_loop () at 003-02-maximum.s:40
    40      cmpq %rdi, %rax         # Compare values.
    (gdb)

This tells you that the program was interrupted by the SIGINT signal
(from your `control-c`), and was within the section labelled
`_start_loop`, and was executing on line 40 when it stopped (the line
numbers are one less than in the book\'s file after the `incq` line,
because that line is missing). It gives you the code that it is about to
execute. Depending on exactly when you hit `control-c`, it may have
stopped on a different line or a different instruction than the
example.

One of the best ways to find bugs in a program is to follow the flow of
the program to see where it is branching incorrectly. To follow the flow
of this program, keep on entering `stepi` (for \"step instruction\"),
which will cause the computer to execute one instruction at a time. If
you do this several times, your output will look something like this:

    (gdb) stepi
    41      jle _start_loop         # Jump to loop beginning if
    (gdb) stepi
    37      cmpq $0, %rax           # Check to see if we have
    (gdb) stepi
    38      je _loop_exit           # hit the end.
    (gdb) stepi
    39      movq (%rbx,%rcx,8), %rax  # Load next value.
    (gdb) stepi
    40      cmpq %rdi, %rax         # Compare values.
    (gdb) stepi
    41      jle _start_loop         # Jump to loop beginning if

As you can tell, it has looped. In general, this is good, since we wrote
it to loop. However, the problem is that it is *never stopping*.
Therefore, to find out what the problem is, let\'s look at the point in
our code where we should be exiting the loop:

```{.gnuassembler}
cmpq $0, %rax
je   _loop_exit
```

Basically, it is checking to see if _%rax_ hits zero. If so, it should
exit the loop. There are several things to check here. First of all, you
may have left this piece out altogether. It is not uncommon for a
programmer to forget to include a way to exit a loop. However, this is
not the case here. Second, you should make sure that `_loop_exit`
actually is outside the loop. If we put the label in the wrong place,
strange things would happen. However, again, this is not the case.

Neither of those potential problems are the culprit. So, the next option
is that perhaps _%rax_ has the wrong value. There are two ways to check
the contents of register in GDB. The first one is the command
`info registers`. This will display the contents of all registers in
hexadecimal and in decimal. However, we are only interested in _%rax_ at
this point. To just display _%rax_ we can do `print $rax`, and add a
format to choose how it is shown: `print/d $rax` prints it in decimal,
`print/x $rax` in hexadecimal, and so on. Notice that in GDB, registers
are prefixed with dollar signs rather than percent signs. Your screen
should have this on it:

    (gdb) print $rax
    $1 = 3
    (gdb) print/d $rax
    $2 = 3
    (gdb) print/t $rax
    $3 = 11
    (gdb) print/o $rax
    $4 = 03
    (gdb) print/x $rax
    $5 = 0x3
    (gdb) print/c $rax
    $6 = 3 '\003'

The formats are `d` (decimal), `t` (binary), `o` (octal), `x`
(hexadecimal) and `c` (character). This means that the result of your
first inquiry is 3. Every inquiry you make will be assigned a number
prefixed with a dollar sign, which you can use in later commands. Now,
if you look back into the code, you will find that 3 is the first
number in the list of numbers to search through. You can see the whole
list with the `x` command, which examines memory: `x/9gd &data_items`
shows 9 giant words (`g`, 8 bytes each) in decimal (`d`), starting at
the address of `data_items`:

    (gdb) x/9gd &data_items
    0x402000:       3       67
    0x402010:       34      222
    0x402020:       45      22
    0x402030:       11      125
    0x402040:       0

If you step through the loop a few more times, you will find that in
every loop iteration _%rax_ has the number 3. This is not what should be
happening. _%rax_ should go to the next value in the list in every
iteration.

Okay, now we know that _%rax_ is being loaded with the same value over
and over again. Let\'s search to see where _%rax_ is being loaded from.
The line of code is this:

```{.gnuassembler}
movq (%rbx,%rcx,8), %rax  # Load next value.
```

So, step until this line of code is ready to execute. Now, this code
depends on two values - _%rbx_ and _%rcx_. _%rbx_ holds the address of
`data_items`, which the program loaded with `leaq` at the beginning and
never changes. It\'s a good idea to check your source code to make sure
the label is in front of the right data, but in our case it is.
Therefore, we need to look at _%rcx_. `info registers` can also show
only the registers you name:

    (gdb) info registers rax rbx rcx rdi rip
    rax            0x3                 3
    rbx            0x402000            4202496
    rcx            0x0                 0
    rdi            0x3                 3
    rip            0x401022            0x401022 <_start_loop+13>

This indicates that _%rcx_ is set to zero, which is why it keeps on
loading the first element of the list. This should cause you to ask
yourself two questions - what is the purpose of _%rcx_, and how should
its value be changed? To answer the first question, we just need to look
in the comments. _%rcx_ is holding the current index of `data_items`.
Since our search is a sequential search through the list of numbers in
`data_items`, it would make sense that _%rcx_ should be incremented with
every loop iteration.

Scanning the code, there is no code which alters _%rcx_ at all.
Therefore, we should add a line to increment _%rcx_ at the beginning of
every loop iteration. This happens to be exactly the line we tossed out
at the beginning. Assembling, linking, and running the program again
will show that it now works correctly.

Let\'s finish the execution typing `quit`. It will ask before killing
the process, because the program is still running (it never exits on
its own); type `y` to kill it and exit from GDB.

Hopefully this exercise provided some insight into using GDB to help you
find errors in your programs.

Breakpoints and Other GDB Features {#breakpoints-and-other-gdb-features}
----------------------------------

The program we entered in the last section had an infinite loop, and
could be easily stopped using `control-c`. Other programs may simply
abort or finish with errors. In these cases, `control-c` doesn\'t help,
because by the time you press `control-c`, the program is already
finished. To fix this, you need to set *breakpoints*. A breakpoint is a
place in the source code that you have marked to indicate to the
debugger that it should stop the program when it hits that point.

To set breakpoints you have to set them up before you run the program.
Before issuing the `run` command, you can set up breakpoints using the
`break` command. For example, to break on line 27, issue the command
`break 27`. Then, when the program crosses line 27, it will stop
running, and print out the current line and instruction. You can then
step through the program from that point and examine registers and
memory. To look at the lines and line numbers of your program, you can
simply use the command `list` (or `l`). This will print out your
program with line numbers, ten lines at a time; `list 25,29` prints
those lines. Let\'s try it with the factorial program of
[Chapter 4. All About Functions](04-all-about-functions.qmd#chapter-4-all-about-functions):

    (gdb) break 27
    Breakpoint 1 at 0x401007: file 004-02-factorial.s, line 27.
    (gdb) run
    Breakpoint 1, _start () at 004-02-factorial.s:27
    27          call factorial          # Run the factorial
    (gdb) list 25,29
    25                                  # want a factorial of. It
    26                                  # goes in %rdi.
    27          call factorial          # Run the factorial
    28                                  # function.
    29

When stepping through code, you often don\'t want to have to step
through every instruction of every function. Well-tested functions are
usually a waste of time to step through except on rare occasion.
Therefore, if you use the `nexti` command instead of the `stepi`
command, GDB will wait until completion of the function before going
on. Otherwise, with `stepi`, GDB would step you through every
instruction within every called function. Here, `nexti` runs the whole
calculation, with all its recursive calls, and stops after the `call`:

    (gdb) nexti
    30          movq %rax, %rdi         # factorial returns the
    (gdb) print $rax
    $1 = 24

The commands `step` and `next` do the same as `stepi` and `nexti`, but
one source line at a time instead of one instruction at a time. In
assembly language, almost every line is one instruction, so they behave
almost the same; in a high-level language, one line can be many
instructions.

When dealing with functions, you can also break on the function names.
In the factorial program, we could set a breakpoint for the factorial
function by typing in `break factorial`. This will cause the debugger to
break every time the function is called, before its first instruction.
To pass arguments to a program, type them after `run`, or use
`set args` before it, as you would on the command line. Let\'s use the
breakpoint to watch the recursion:

    (gdb) break factorial
    Breakpoint 1 at 0x401018: file 004-02-factorial.s, line 44.
    (gdb) run
    Breakpoint 1, factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:44
    44          pushq %rbp              # Standard function stuff
    (gdb) print $rdi
    $1 = 4
    (gdb) print (long)$rsp % 16
    $2 = 8

The parameter is 4, in _%rdi_. The second command checks the alignment
rule of Chapter 4: when a function starts, the `call` has just pushed
the 8-byte return address, so _%rsp_ is 8 more than a multiple of 16.
Now type `continue` three times: each time the program runs until the
next call to `factorial`, and prints the same two lines as the first
breakpoint (we show them only once). Then print _%rdi_ again, and ask
for a *backtrace*, the list of functions that are waiting for a return:

    (gdb) continue
    Breakpoint 1, factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:44
    44          pushq %rbp              # Standard function stuff
    (gdb) print $rdi
    $3 = 1
    (gdb) backtrace
    #0  factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:44
    #1  0x0000000000401035 in factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:66
    #2  0x0000000000401035 in factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:66
    #3  0x0000000000401035 in factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:66
    #4  0x000000000040100c in _start () at 004-02-factorial.s:27

This is the recursion of Chapter 4, seen from inside: `_start` called
`factorial(4)`, which called `factorial(3)`, which called
`factorial(2)`, which called `factorial(1)`, where we are now. Each line
shows the return address of one frame (`0x401035` is the instruction
after the recursive `call`), and gdb finds them by following the chain
of saved _%rbp_ values (see
[The Frame Pointer](12-optimization.qmd#the-frame-pointer)). `finish`
runs until the current function returns, and stops in its caller:

    (gdb) finish
    factorial () at 004-02-factorial.s:68
    68          imulq -8(%rbp), %rax    # Multiply our number by
    (gdb) print $rax
    $4 = 1
    (gdb) info frame
    Stack level 0, frame at 0x7fffffffecd0:
     rip = 0x401035 in factorial (004-02-factorial.s:68); saved rip = 0x401035
     called by frame at 0x7fffffffecf0
     source language asm.
     Arglist at 0x7fffffffecc0, args:
     Locals at 0x7fffffffecc0, Previous frame's sp is 0x7fffffffecd0
     Saved registers:
      rbp at 0x7fffffffecc0, rip at 0x7fffffffecc8

`factorial(1)` returned 1, and we are back in `factorial(2)`, about to
multiply. `info frame` describes the current frame: where the caller\'s
_%rbp_ and the return address are saved, 0 and 8 bytes above our _%rbp_.
Notice the addresses near 0x7fffffffffff: gdb turns ASLR off by default
(see
[Chapter 9](09-intermediate-memory-topics.qmd#address-space-layout-randomization)),
so they are the same in every session.

### The Text User Interface {#the-text-user-interface}

GDB can also divide the terminal into windows, to show the source code
(or the instructions) and the registers while you step. Start it with
`gdb -tui`, or type these commands in a session:

-   `layout src` shows the source code, with the current line marked.

-   `layout asm` shows the instructions, as `objdump -d` would.

-   `layout regs` adds a window with the registers, which highlights the
    ones that the last instruction changed.

-   `tui disable` goes back to the normal mode, and `control-l` redraws
    the screen if the program\'s output messed it up.

---

> **TIP.**
>
> GDB uses the AT&T syntax by default, like this book. If you prefer
  the Intel syntax, type `set disassembly-flavor intel` (see
  [Appendix B](appendix-b-common-x86-instructions.qmd#differences-in-other-syntaxes-and-terminology)).
  Floating-point registers are printed with `print $xmm0`, and
  `print $xmm0.v2_double[0]` shows the `double` in its lowest 8 bytes.

---

GDB Quick-Reference {#gdb-quick-reference}
-------------------

This [quick-reference table][AF-Reference] is copyright 2002
[Robert M. Dondero, Jr.][AF-Donero], and is used by permission in this
book. Parameters listed in brackets are optional. Here is another
[GDB quick reference][AF-GDB-reference] created by
[Free Software Foundation][AF-FSF].

Table F-1. Common GDB Debugging Commands

### Miscellaneous {#miscellaneous}

quit

> Exit GDB.

help \[cmd\]

> Print description of debugger command `cmd`.  Without `cmd`, prints
  a list of topics.

directory \[dir1\] \[dir2\]...

> Add directories `dir1`, `dir2`, etc. to the list of directories
  searched for source files.

### Running the Program {#running-the-program}

run \[arg1\] \[arg2\]...

> Run the program with command line arguments `arg1`, `arg2`, etc.

set args arg1 \[arg2\]...

> Set the program\'s command-line arguments to `arg1`, `arg2`, etc.

show args

> Print the program\'s command-line arguments.

### Using Breakpoints {#using-breakpoints}

info breakpoints

> Print a list of all breakpoints and their numbers (breakpoint numbers
  are used for other breakpoint commands).

break _linenum_

> Set a breakpoint at line number _linenum_.

break \*_addr_

> Set a breakpoint at memory address _addr_.

break _fn_

> Set a breakpoint at the beginning of function _fn_.

condition _bpnum_ _expr_

> Break at breakpoint _bpnum_ only if expression _expr_ is non-zero.

command \[_bpnum_\] _cmd1_ \[_cmd2_\]...

> Execute commands `cmd1`, `cmd2`, etc. whenever breakpoint _bpnum_
  (or the current breakpoint) is hit.

continue

>  Continue executing the program.

kill

> Stop executing the program.

delete \[_bpnum1_\] \[_bpnum2_\]...

> Delete breakpoints _bpnum1_, _bpnum2_, etc., or all breakpoints if
  none specified.

clear \*_addr_

> Clear the breakpoint at memory address _addr_.

clear \[_fn_\]

> Clear the breakpoint at function _fn_, or the current breakpoint.

clear _linenum_

> Clear the breakpoint at line number _linenum_.

disable \[_bpnum1_\] \[_bpnum2_\]...

> Disable breakpoints _bpnum1_, _bpnum2_, etc., or all breakpoints if
  none specified.

enable \[_bpnum1_\] \[_bpnum2_\]...

> Enable breakpoints _bpnum1_, _bpnum2_, etc., or all breakpoints if
  none specified.

### Stepping through the Program {#stepping-through-the-program}

nexti

> \"Step over\" the next instruction (doesn\'t follow function calls).

stepi

> \"Step into\" the next instruction (follows function calls).

next, step

> The same as `nexti` and `stepi`, one source line at a time.

finish

> \"Step out\" of the current function.

layout src, layout asm, layout regs

> Show the source, the instructions or the registers in windows of
  the text user interface (`tui disable` closes them).

### Examining Registers and Memory {#examining-registers-and-memory}

info registers \[_reg1_\] \[_reg2_\]...

> Print the contents of all registers, or only of the given ones (for
  example `info registers rax rdi`).

print/_f_ _$reg_

> Print the contents of register _$reg_ using format _f_. The format
  can be _x_ (hexadecimal), _d_ (decimal), _u_ (unsigned decimal), _t_
  (binary), _o_ (octal), _a_ (address), _c_ (character), _s_ (string),
  or _f_ (floating point).

x/_rsf_ _addr_

> Print the contents of memory address _addr_ using repeat count _r_,
  size _s_, and format _f_. Repeat count defaults to 1 if not
  specified. Size can be _b_ (byte), _h_ (halfword, 2 bytes), _w_
  (word, 4 bytes), or _g_ (giant, 8 bytes). Size defaults to the last
  one used. Format is the same as for print, with the additions of _s_
  (string) and _i_ (instruction). For example `x/5i $rip` displays the
  next 5 instructions, `x/8xb $rsp` the 8 bytes at the top of the
  stack in hexadecimal, and `x/s $rsi` the string that _%rsi_ points
  to.

info display

> Shows a numbered list of expressions set up to display automatically
  at each break.

display/_f_ _$reg_

> At each break, print the contents of register _reg_ using format _f_.

display/_si_ _addr_

> At each break, print the contents of memory address _addr_ using
  size _s_ (same options as for the x command).

display/_ss_ _addr_

> At each break, print the string of size _s_ that begins in memory
  address _addr_.

undisplay _displaynum_

> Remove _displaynum_ from the display list.

### Examining the Call Stack {#examining-the-call-stack}

info frame

> Print where the current frame saved the registers and the return
  address.

where

> Print the call stack.

backtrace

> Print the call stack.

frame

> Print the top of the call stack.

up

> Move the context toward the bottom of the call stack.

down

> Move the context toward the top of the call stack.
